title: Air in the system
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: At 1:40 p.m., the air detector alarms on Mrs. Nora Valdez’s machine. You see foam below the venous chamber. She is sitting up and suddenly coughs and says her chest feels tight. You are her nurse.

choices.text: Keep the pump stopped, clamp the venous line, do not return the blood.
choices.feedback: Air on the patient side is an emergency; returning the blood pushes more air in. Never override the air detector.

choices.text: Clear the alarm and complete the rinse-back, so the blood in the circuit is not lost.
choices.feedback: Overriding the detector and rinsing back drives air into the patient.
choices.then: The charge nurse stops the rinse-back and clamps.

choices.text: Tap the chamber to move the bubbles up, check the level, and restart the pump slowly.
choices.feedback: Air below the venous chamber is not removed by tapping; restarting risks embolism.

n2.prompt: How do you position and support her?

choices.text: 100% oxygen; flat per protocol (never sitting up); call for help and arrange transfer.
choices.feedback: AHA 2025: 100% oxygen (COR 1) and supine or recovery position on a level surface (COR 2a); dialysis teaching uses the left side. Never sitting up. Supine or left side per the unit protocol; call the cart, the physician-on-duty and the attending; emergency transfer.

choices.text: Sit her upright to ease the breathing and give oxygen by nasal cannula while you call the physician.
choices.feedback: Sitting up can send air to the brain; every source says never sit up.

n3.scene: She becomes unresponsive with gasping. No pulse.

choices.text: Cardiac arrest: CPR flat on her back; circuit clamped, blood not returned.
choices.feedback: Every source agrees CPR is done flat on the back. The blood decision stays “not returned.” Pads and the arrest algorithm as usual.

choices.text: Keep her on her left side while compressing, so the air stays trapped away from the outflow of the heart.
choices.feedback: Effective compressions need her flat on her back.
choices.then: The team turns her supine and compresses.

n4.scene: The technician wants to inspect the circuit.

choices.text: Keep the circuit clamped and intact; the machine is held for the biomedical technician.
choices.feedback: Finding the air entry point prevents the next event. The technician checks the detector and clamp before the machine is used again.

choices.text: Discard the lines and clean the station so the next patient on the list can start on time.
choices.feedback: The evidence of the entry point is lost.

end.title: 2:10 p.m.
end.text: Mrs. Valdez regains a pulse and is transferred for oxygen therapy and assessment for hyperbaric treatment. The entry point is found: a loose connection before the blood pump.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Air: clamp, do not return, 100% oxygen, flat, never sitting up.
  • Position differs between sources; follow the unit protocol. CPR is always flat on the back.
  • Keep the circuit for inspection.
